summary: Core engineer on a 15-service TypeScript monorepo for an AI-powered mortgage-lending platform, working across backend services, frontend, and infrastructure.
highlights: Originated and shipped the production LLM extraction service that reads the documents the incumbent OCR vendor classifies but never extracts — in production since February 2026. Mine from the first commit: the rearchitecture into three independently retriable message-bus consumers, the migration off a hosted LLM gateway onto direct provider APIs, and the multi-provider failover package it now shares with other services.

Ran the vendor-replacement evaluation as a proof of concept — eight rounds over four weeks, sole author, never shipped — and reported every figure with its sample size: 94.0% segment F1 and 95.6% page-assignment accuracy on document splitting (n=250 ground-truth documents, deterministic scoring, no judge), 88.4% exact document type and 95.0% type family (n=242), and 74.7% field-reading correctness over the 48% of the answer key the scorer could compare (n=202), at about $0.30 per loan against the incumbent vendor's flat $25. Ground truth was drafted by review agents reading every page against the production extraction, then reviewed and accuracy-confirmed by the operations team, plus a deterministic hygiene audit over the answer key itself.

Traced document classification failures to the vocabulary rather than the model: free-text type naming matched the target vocabulary 14.3% of the time, while the same model constrained to a closed 81-type enum reached 82.4% — a fix to the output contract, not a bigger model. I also withdrew my own round-one headline once a second corpus showed it was corpus bias, and rebuilt the case on coverage and cost instead.

Created the platform's communication infrastructure and remain its main owner — 57.6% of its current source by surviving-line blame, 568 of its 1,048 commits, and sole author for its first four months. Asynchronous email sync driven off a message bus, LLM-driven message classification, and a loan-matching core that is channel-agnostic: SMS, calls and voicemail reuse it unchanged by normalising into the same subject/body/sender shape.

Kept deterministic loan matching strictly separated from non-deterministic LLM classification. The matcher — built by another team over field-level-encrypted borrower data — sits behind a service boundary reached through a flat, primitive-only contract that no prompt, model output or confidence score ever crosses; I built the extraction side that feeds it, and classification runs after matching and never into it.

Built a Redis and Lua distributed sliding-window rate limiter with an atomic dual-key script covering a global budget and per-endpoint tiers, deliberately set at 80% of each vendor's published limits so a burst degrades into local queueing instead of rejected calls — later extracted into a shared package other services now use.

Built the telephony vertical end to end: HMAC-verified webhook handling with a replay window and timing-safe comparison, the domain layer, the provider client, rate limiting and the enrichment consumer — plus an SMS debounce that collapses a burst into a single conversation using a quiet-period window keyed on the sorted phone pair, drained by a scheduled worker with a compare-and-delete Lua script so a message arriving between scan and delete cannot be lost.

Made third-party sync failures resumable rather than blindly retried: a durable retry worker where each failure records the stage it failed at and the replay picks up from that checkpoint, re-running only the messages that actually failed.

Built a tenant- and loan-scoped vector search layer over conversation history — every query is filtered on both tenant and loan, never searched globally — with token-budget-aware truncation before embedding, so long messages are trimmed against a real token count rather than a character guess.

Own the document-analysis side of the platform's loan analysis system — the checks, the LLM layer, the evaluation lane and the pipeline they run on, including the architecture decisions behind its current shape. I created roughly 45-50 of about 67 production checks and re-architected analysis from a monolith into a three-stage event pipeline. Every production check is deterministic code: I made the call to replace flaky LLM-based checks with deterministic ones and confine the LLM to bounded, non-blocking roles.

Built an inbound-communication agent workflow end to end — it reads lender email, maps the classification onto loan milestone dates, and proposes the update. Nothing that touches a customer or the loan record is applied without a human approving it; internal bookkeeping auto-applies behind per-action confidence thresholds.

Led evaluation infrastructure for the platform's LLM features: created the agent evaluation harness, authored the file-naming convention and the CI gate that only spends real-model budget when a prompt or an agent actually changes, and proposed opposing-provider judging off the back of that research — an OpenAI model grading OpenAI output flatters itself. I wrote it into the engineering standards, implemented it end to end in a second service's evaluation lane, and led the team that built the LLM-as-a-judge scorers, alongside per-call cost tracing and version-controlled prompt assets.

Designed and delivered a monorepo-wide, agent-consumable documentation system with deterministic integrity gates in CI, alongside broad ownership of shared packages, public upload flows, user offboarding, observability, and production incident response.
